Efforts to resolve the Israeli–Palestinian conflict

Intermittent discussions are held by various parties and proposals put forward in an attempt to resolve the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict") through a [peace process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_process "Peace process").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-1) Since the 1970s, there has been a parallel effort made to find terms upon which peace can be agreed to in both this conflict and the wider [Arab–Israeli conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_conflict "Arab–Israeli conflict"). Notably, the [Camp David Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_David_Accords "Camp David Accords") between [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") included discussions on plans for Palestinian autonomy, but did not include any Palestinian representatives. The autonomy plan was not implemented, but its stipulations were represented to a large extent in the [Oslo Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Accords "Oslo Accords").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Rashid_Khalidi-2)

Despite the failure of the peace process to produce a final agreement, the international consensus has for decades supported a [two-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-state_solution "Two-state solution") to the conflict, based on [United Nations Security Council Resolution 242](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_242 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 242") and [338](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_338 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 338"). This includes the establishment of an independent Palestinian state under the [pre-1967 borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Israel) "Green Line (Israel)") including [East Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Jerusalem "East Jerusalem") and a resolution to the refugee question based on the [Palestinian right of return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_right_of_return "Palestinian right of return") (in accordance with [United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_Resolution_194 "United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194"), though Israel disputes this interpretation).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Norman_G._Finkelstein-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFarah2013160-4) This is in contrast to the current situation under the Oslo Accords in which the [Palestinian territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_territories "Palestinian territories") are [divided into areas of varying jurisdiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_occupation_of_the_West_Bank#Territorial_fragmentation_and_domination_over_the_Palestinians "Israeli occupation of the West Bank") between Israeli military control and the [Palestinian National Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_National_Authority "Palestinian National Authority") (PA), with the PA only having partial self-rule in [Area A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_A "Area A") of the West Bank and in the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip"). A final settlement as stipulated by the Oslo Accords has yet to be reached.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-5)

## Background

For the United States and Israel, the [Palestine Liberation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_Liberation_Organization "Palestine Liberation Organization") (PLO)'s participation in diplomatic negotiations was dependent on its complete disavowal of political violence and full recognition of Israel's "right to exist". This stipulation required the PLO to abandon its objective of reclaiming all of historic Palestine and instead focus on the 22 percent which came under Israeli military control in 1967.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-hc_baconi-6) By the late 1970s, Palestinian leadership in the occupied territories and most Arab states supported a two-state settlement.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-mishal_sela-7) In 1981, Saudi Arabia put forward a plan based on a two-state settlement to the conflict with support from the Arab League.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-8) Israeli analyst Avner Yaniv describes Arafat as ready to make a historic compromise at this time, while the Israeli cabinet continued to oppose the existence of a Palestinian state. Yaniv described Arafat's willingness to compromise as a "peace offensive" which Israel responded to by planning to remove the PLO as a potential negotiating partner in order to evade international diplomatic pressure.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Avner_Yaniv-9) Israel would invade Lebanon the following year in an attempt to undermine the PLO as a political organization, weakening Palestinian nationalism and facilitating the annexation of the West Bank into Greater Israel.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-10)

While the PLO had adopted a program of pursuing a Palestinian state alongside Israel since the mid-1970s, the 1988 [Palestinian Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Declaration_of_Independence "Palestinian Declaration of Independence") formally consecrated this objective. This declaration, which was based on resolutions from the Palestine National Council sessions in the late 1970s and 1980s, advocated for the creation of a Palestinian state comprising the West Bank, Gaza Strip, and East Jerusalem, within the borders set by the 1949 armistice lines prior to June 5, 1967. Following the declaration, Arafat explicitly denounced all forms of terrorism and affirmed the PLO's acceptance of UN Resolutions 242 and 338, as well as the recognition of Israel's right to exist. All the conditions defined by Henry Kissinger for US negotiations with the PLO had now been met.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-11)

Israeli prime minister [Yitzhak Shamir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Shamir "Yitzhak Shamir") stood behind the stance that the PLO was a terrorist organization and would not accept it as a negotiating partner. He maintained a strict stance against any concessions, including withdrawal from occupied Palestinian territories, recognition of or negotiations with the PLO, and especially the establishment of a Palestinian state. Shamir viewed the U.S. decision to engage in dialogue with the PLO as a mistake that threatened the existing territorial status quo. He argued that negotiating with the PLO meant accepting the existence of a Palestinian state and hence was unacceptable.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-12)

The term "peace-process" refers to the step-by-step approach to resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Having originally entered into usage to describe the US mediated negotiations between Israel and surrounding Arab countries, notably Egypt, the term "peace-process" has grown to be associated with an emphasis on the negotiation process rather than on presenting a comprehensive solution to the conflict.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPapp%C3%A92022-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-William_B._Quandt-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhalidi2020-15) As part of this process, fundamental issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict such as borders, access to resources, and the Palestinian right of return, have been left to "final status" talks. Such "final status" negotiations along the lines discussed in Madrid in 1991 have never taken place.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhalidi2020-15)

### Peace efforts with confrontation states

Main article: [Arab–Israeli normalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_normalization "Arab–Israeli normalization")

There were parallel efforts for peace treaties between Israel and other "confrontation states": Egypt, Jordan and Syria after the [Six-Day war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_war "Six-Day war"), and Lebanon afterwards.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Education2006-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-SayighShlaim1997-17) UN resolution 242 was accepted by Israel, Jordan, and Egypt, but rejected by Syria until 1972–1973.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-18)

In 1970, [US Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Secretary_of_State "US Secretary of State") [William P. Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_P._Rogers "William P. Rogers") proposed the [Rogers Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogers_Plan "Rogers Plan"), which called for a 90-day cease-fire, a military standstill zone on each side of the Suez Canal, and an effort to reach agreement in the framework of [UN Resolution 242](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_242 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 242"). [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") rejected the plan on 10 December 1969, calling it "an attempt to appease \[the Arabs\] at the expense of Israel". The Soviets dismissed it as "one-sided" and "pro-Israeli". [President Nasser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser "Gamal Abdel Nasser") rejected it because it was a separate deal with Israel even if [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") recovered all of [Sinai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinai_Peninsula "Sinai Peninsula").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Morris2011p354-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-20)

### 1949 Armistice Agreements

Main article: [1949 Armistice Agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Armistice_Agreements "1949 Armistice Agreements")

The [1947–1948 civil war in Mandatory Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1947%E2%80%931948_civil_war_in_Mandatory_Palestine "1947–1948 civil war in Mandatory Palestine") followed by the [1948 Arab–Israeli War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_War "1948 Arab–Israeli War") all ended with the February–July [1949 Armistice Agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Armistice_Agreements "1949 Armistice Agreements") between [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") and [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt"), [Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon "Lebanon"), [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan"), and [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria"). Those Arab countries insisted explicitly in the agreement texts that the agreed Armistice Demarcation Lines ('Green Lines') should not be construed as political or territorial boundaries, thus aiming to safeguard the [right of return of those Palestinians that had fled their homes during the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_right_of_return "Palestinian right of return"), and the illegitimacy of Israel's use or appropriation of abandoned Palestinian property.

After the 1967 [Six-Day War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War "Six-Day War"), in which Israel had conquered, among more, the Palestinian [West Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bank "West Bank") and [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip") in a pre-emptive surprise-strike against overtly hostile Arab neighbouring countries, top Israeli leaders like Golda Meir, Menachem Begin and Abba Eban have emphasized that returning to the pre-1967 borders would be extremely dangerous for Israel, bordering on "national suicide".

### Geneva, December 1973

Main article: [Geneva Conference (1973)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Conference_(1973) "Geneva Conference (1973)")

After the ceasefire on 25 October 1973 ending the [Yom Kippur War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War "Yom Kippur War") (surprise attack on Israel on 6 October by Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Iraq assisted by more countries), the U.S. and U.S.S.R. [gathered the foreign ministers of Israel, Egypt and Jordan in Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Conference_(1973) "Geneva Conference (1973)") in December 1973 to pursue "peace", firstly disengagement of armed forces, towards fulfilling [UNSC Resolution 242](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_242 "UN 242") dating from 1967 ("…the need to work for a just and lasting peace in the Middle East in which every State in the area can live in security"). Syria had refused to show up because Israel and the US refused to invite the [PLO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLO "PLO"). The short conference facilitated a reconciliation between Israel, Egypt, and Syria, but achieved nothing for the Palestinians.

### Camp David, 1978

Main article: [Camp David Accords §Framework for Peace in the Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_David_Accords#Framework_for_Peace_in_the_Middle_East "Camp David Accords")

A political agreement was signed between Israel and Egypt (notably excluding representatives from the PLO) in 1978, aiming to establish a self-governing authority in the West Bank and Gaza and autonomy for the inhabitants of those lands, as an attempt towards "Peace in the Middle East". "Autonomy" in this case would not mean "self-determination"; Israeli Prime Minister [Menachem Begin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Begin "Menachem Begin") specifically insisted that "on no condition will there be a Palestinian state".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Khalidi,2013-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Filiu2014-22)

Meanwhile, Egypt's status as the strongest Arab nation capable of challenging Israel militarily meant that its parallel withdrawal from the Arab-Israeli conflict in the [Egypt–Israel peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt%E2%80%93Israel_peace_treaty "Egypt–Israel peace treaty") (March 1979) significantly weakened the collective military and diplomatic power of the other Arab countries. It has been argued that this shift essentially eliminated Israel's motivation to make concessions in the West Bank, Gaza, or other areas.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-23)

### Madrid (1991–1993)

Main article: [Madrid Conference of 1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Conference_of_1991 "Madrid Conference of 1991")

Delegations from Israel, Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan accepted the invitation from US President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") and the Soviet Union president [Mikhail Gorbachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev "Mikhail Gorbachev") to attend the [Madrid Conference of 1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Conference_of_1991 "Madrid Conference of 1991"),[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-24) after the [First Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-25)

### Oslo (1993–2001)

Main article: [Oslo Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Accords "Oslo Accords")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Bill_Clinton%2C_Yitzhak_Rabin%2C_Yasser_Arafat_at_the_White_House_1993-09-13.jpg/330px-Bill_Clinton%2C_Yitzhak_Rabin%2C_Yasser_Arafat_at_the_White_House_1993-09-13.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Clinton,_Yitzhak_Rabin,_Yasser_Arafat_at_the_White_House_1993-09-13.jpg) [Yitzhak Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Rabin "Yitzhak Rabin"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), and [Yasser Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat "Yasser Arafat") at the Oslo Accords signing ceremony on 13 September 1993

While the slow moving Madrid talks were taking place, a series of secret meetings between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators were taking place in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), which resulted in the [1993 Oslo Peace Accords between Palestinians and Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Oslo_Peace_Accords_between_Palestinians_and_Israel "1993 Oslo Peace Accords between Palestinians and Israel"), a plan discussing the necessary elements and conditions for a future [Palestinian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_state "Palestinian state") "on the basis of [Security Council Resolutions 242](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_242 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 242") and [338](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_338 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 338")".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-26) The agreement, officially titled the [Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Principles_on_Interim_Self-Government_Arrangements "Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements") (DOP), was signed on the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") lawn on 13 September 1993. The stipulations of the Oslo agreements were criticized\[ _[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] as diverging from prevailing interpretations of how the conflict should be resolved; critics\[ _[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] argued that the agreements failed to guarantee Palestinian self-determination or statehood and departed from one interpretation of UN Resolution 242, which holds that land cannot be acquired by war.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-pop_christison-27) Political analyst Noam Chomsky argued that the Oslo agreements allowed Israel "to do virtually what it likes".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-ft_Chomsky-28) Other observers, however, viewed the accords as a breakthrough that created a framework for mutual recognition and negotiations.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-30)

Various "transfers of power and responsibilities" in the Gaza Strip and West Bank from Israel to the Palestinians took place in the mid-1990s.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-31) Israeli foreign minister Shlomo Ben-Ami described the Oslo Accords as legitimizing "the transformation of the West Bank into what has been called a 'cartographic cheeseboard'". Indeed, Oslo legitimized the fragmentation of Palestinian population centers by Jewish-only settlements and bypass roads, Israeli checkpoints, and military installations.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-sowwop-32) Core to the Oslo Accords was the creation of the Palestinian Authority and the security cooperation it would enter into with the Israeli military authorities. Ben-Ami, who participated in the Camp David 2000 talks, described this process: "One of the meanings of Oslo was that the PLO was eventually Israel's collaborator in the task of stifling the Intifada and cutting short what was clearly an authentically democratic struggle for Palestinian independence."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-sowwop-32)

After the assassination of [Yitzhak Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Rabin "Yitzhak Rabin") in 1995, the peace process eventually ground to a halt. The settlements' population almost doubled in the West Bank. Later [suicide bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_bombing "Suicide bombing") attacks from Palestinian militant groups and the subsequent retaliatory actions from the [Israeli military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_military "Israeli military") made conditions for peace negotiations untenable.

### 1996–1999 agreements

Newly elected Prime Minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") declared a new policy following the many suicide attacks by [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas") and [Palestinian Islamic Jihad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Islamic_Jihad "Palestinian Islamic Jihad") since 1993, including a [wave of suicide attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem_bus_18_massacres#Wave_of_attacks "Jerusalem bus 18 massacres") before the [Israeli elections of May 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Israeli_general_election "1996 Israeli general election"). Netanyahu declared a [tit-for-tat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tit-for-tat "Tit-for-tat") policy which he termed "reciprocity", whereby Israel would not engage in the peace process if Arafat continued with what Netanyahu defined as the [Palestinian revolving door policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolving_door_policy_(alleged_Palestinian_Authority_policy) "Revolving door policy (alleged Palestinian Authority policy)"), i.e., incitement and direct or indirect support of terrorism. The [Hebron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron_Agreement "Hebron Agreement") and [Wye Agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Agreement "Wye Agreement") were signed during this period, after Israel considered that its conditions were partially met.

The Protocol Concerning the Redeployment in Hebron, also known as the Hebron Protocol or [Hebron Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron_Agreement "Hebron Agreement"), began on 7 January and was concluded between Israel and the [PLO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLO "PLO") from 15 to 17 January 1997. The agreement dealt with the redeployment of Israeli military forces in Hebron in accordance with the Oslo Accords, security issues, and other concerns.

The [Wye River Memorandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_River_Memorandum "Wye River Memorandum") was a political agreement negotiated to implement the Oslo Accords, completed on 23 October 1998. It was signed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat. It was negotiated at Wye River, Maryland (at the Wye River Conference Center) and signed at the White House with President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") as the official witness. On 17 November 1998, Israel's 120-member parliament, the [Knesset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knesset "Knesset"), approved the Memorandum by voting 75–19. The agreement dealt with further redeployments in the West Bank, security issues, and other concerns. Major international human rights organizations criticized the memorandum for its "encouragement" of human rights abuses.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-34)

### Camp David 2000 Summit, Clinton's "Parameters", and the Taba talks

Main article: [2000 Camp David Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Camp_David_Summit "2000 Camp David Summit")

In 2000, US President Bill Clinton convened a peace summit between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister [Ehud Barak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehud_Barak "Ehud Barak"). In May of that year, according to [Nathan Thrall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Thrall "Nathan Thrall"), Israel had offered Palestinians 66% of the West Bank, with 17% annexed to Israel, and a further 17% not annexed but under Israeli control, and no compensating swap of Israeli territory.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Thrall-35) The Israeli prime minister offered the Palestinian leader between 91%[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-36) and 95%[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-37)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-38) (sources differ on the exact percentage) of the West Bank and the entire Gaza Strip if 69 Jewish settlements (which comprise 85% of the West Bank's Jewish settlers) were ceded to Israel. [East Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Jerusalem "East Jerusalem") would have fallen for the most part[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-39) under Israeli sovereignty, with the exception of most suburbs with heavy non-Jewish populations surrounded by areas annexed to Israel.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-40) The issue of the [Palestinian right of return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_right_of_return "Palestinian right of return") would be solved through significant monetary reparations.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-41)

Arafat rejected this offer and did not propose a counteroffer.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Ross-42)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-43)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Hirsh-44) No tenable solution was crafted which would satisfy both Israeli and Palestinian demands, even under intense U.S. pressure.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Ross-42) Clinton blamed Arafat for the failure of the Camp David Summit.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Ross-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Hirsh-44) In the months following the summit, Clinton appointed former [US Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senator "US Senator") [George J. Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_J._Mitchell "George J. Mitchell") to lead a fact-finding committee that later published the [Mitchell Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Report_(Arab-Israeli_conflict) "Mitchell Report (Arab-Israeli conflict)").

Proposed in the fall of 2000 following the collapse of the Camp David talks, [The Clinton Parameters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clinton_Parameters "The Clinton Parameters") included a plan on which the Palestinian State was to include 94-96% of the West Bank. Around 80% of the [settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_settlement "Israeli settlement") were to become under Israeli sovereignty. In exchange for that, Israel would concede some territory (so-called 'Territory Exchange' or 'Land Swap') within the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Israel) "Green Line (Israel)") (1967 borders). The swap would consist of 1–3% of Israeli territory, such that the final borders of the West Bank part of the Palestinian state would include 97% of the land of the original borders.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-45)

At the [Taba summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taba_summit "Taba summit") (at [Taba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taba_(Egypt) "Taba (Egypt)")) in January 2001, talks continued based on the Clinton Parameters. The Israeli negotiation team presented a new map. The proposition removed the "temporarily Israeli-controlled" areas from the West Bank and offered a few thousand more refugees than they offered at Camp David to settle into Israel, and hoped that this would be considered "implementation" of [United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_Resolution_194 "United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194").[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-46)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-47) The Palestinian side accepted this as a basis for further negotiation. However, Barak did not conduct further negotiations at that time; the talks ended without an agreement, and the following month, the [right-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing "Right-wing") [Likud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likud "Likud") party candidate [Ariel Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Sharon "Ariel Sharon") was elected Israeli prime minister in February 2001.

### The Arab peace initiative and the Roadmap (2002-03)

Main articles: [Arab Peace Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Peace_Initiative "Arab Peace Initiative"), [Road map for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_map_for_peace "Road map for peace"), and [Beirut Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut_Summit "Beirut Summit")

The Beirut summit of Arab government leaders took place in March 2002 under the aegis of the [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League"). The summit concluded by presenting a plan to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. [Israeli Foreign Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Foreign_Minister "Israeli Foreign Minister") [Shimon Peres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimon_Peres "Shimon Peres") welcomed it and said, "... the details of every peace plan must be discussed directly between Israel and the Palestinians, and to make this possible, the [Palestinian Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Authority "Palestinian Authority") must put an end to terror, the horrifying expression of which we witnessed just last night in [Netanya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netanya "Netanya")",[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-48) referring to the [Netanya suicide attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netanya_suicide_attack "Netanya suicide attack") perpetrated on the previous evening which the Beirut Summit failed to address. Israel was not prepared to enter negotiations as called for by the Arab League plan on the grounds that it did not wish for "full withdrawal to [1967 borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_borders "1967 borders") and the [right of return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_return "Right of return") for the [Palestinian refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_refugees "Palestinian refugees")".[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-49)

Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), center, discusses the peace process with Prime Minister [Ariel Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Sharon "Ariel Sharon") of Israel, left, and Palestinian President [Mahmoud Abbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Abbas "Mahmoud Abbas") in [Aqaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqaba "Aqaba"), Jordan, 4 June 2003.

### Israeli–Palestinian talks in 2007 and 2008

Further information: [Annapolis Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapolis_Conference "Annapolis Conference")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Realignment_plan_map_original.png/250px-Realignment_plan_map_original.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Realignment_plan_map_original.png) Olmert plan, publicised by Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert in February 2025

From December 2006 to mid-September 2008, Israeli Prime Minister [Ehud Olmert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehud_Olmert "Ehud Olmert") and President Mahmoud Abbas of the Palestinian Authority met 36 times; there were also lower-level talks. In 2007, Olmert welcomed the [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League")'s re-endorsement of the [Arab Peace Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Peace_Initiative "Arab Peace Initiative"). In his bid to negotiate a peace accord and establish a Palestinian state, Olmert proposed a plan to the Palestinians.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Plan_for_Peace-50) The centerpiece of Olmert's detailed proposal is the suggested permanent border, which would be based on an Israeli withdrawal from most of the West Bank. Olmert proposed annexing at least 6.3% of Palestinian territory, in exchange for 5.8% of Israeli land, with Palestinians receiving alternative land in the Negev, adjacent to the Gaza Strip, as well as a territorial link, under Israeli sovereignty, for free passage between Gaza and the West Bank. Israel insisted on retaining an armed presence in the future Palestinian state.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Thrall-35)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Olmerts_offer-51) Under Abbas's offer, more than 60 percent of settlers would stay in place. For his part, Olmert presented a plan in which the most sparsely populated settlements would be evacuated. Olmert and Abbas both acknowledged that reciprocal relations would be necessary, not hermetic separation. They also acknowledged the need to share a single business ecosystem, while cooperating intensively on water, security, bandwidth, banking, tourism, and much more. Regarding Jerusalem the leaders agreed that Jewish neighborhoods should remain under Israeli sovereignty and Arab neighborhoods would revert to Palestinian sovereignty.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Plan_for_Peace-50) The Palestinians asked for clarifications of the territorial land swap since they were unable to ascertain what land his percentages affected, since Israeli and Palestinian calculations of the West Bank differ by several hundred square kilometres. For them, in lieu of such clarifications, Olmert's 6.3–6.8% annexation might work out closer to 8.5%, 4 times the 1.9% limit the Palestinians argued a swap should not exceed.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Thrall-35) The talks ended with both sides claiming the other side dropped follow-up contacts.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Thrall-35)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Olmerts_offer-51)

[Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Egypt "Government of Egypt") brokered the [2008 Israel–Hamas ceasefire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Israel%E2%80%93Hamas_ceasefire "2008 Israel–Hamas ceasefire"), which lasted half a year beginning on 19 June 2008 and lasted until 19 December 2008.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-NYTimes-truce-52) The collapse of the ceasefire led to the [Gaza War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_War_(2008%E2%80%9309) "Gaza War (2008–09)") on 27 December 2008.

### 2010 direct talks

Main article: [2010–2011 Israeli–Palestinian peace talks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%932011_Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_talks "2010–2011 Israeli–Palestinian peace talks")

See also: [2010 Palestinian militancy campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Palestinian_militancy_campaign "2010 Palestinian militancy campaign")

In June 2009, reacting to US President Barack Obama's [Cairo Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Beginning_(speech) "A New Beginning (speech)"),[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Thrall-35) Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared for the first time[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-53) conditional support for a future Palestinian state[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-54) but insisted that the Palestinians would need to make reciprocal gestures and accept several principles: recognition of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people; demilitarization of a future Palestinian state, along with additional security guarantees, including defensible borders for Israel;[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-55) acceptance that Jerusalem would remain the united capital of Israel; and renunciation of their claim to a [right of return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_return "Right of return"). He also claimed that Israeli settlements retain the right to growth and expansion in the West Bank. Palestinians rejected the proposals immediately.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-56) In September 2010, the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_administration "Obama administration") pushed to revive the stalled peace process by getting the parties involved to agree to direct talks for the first time in about two years.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-ap090110-57) While U.S. President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was the orchestrator of the movement, U.S. Secretary of State [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") went through months of cajoling just to get the parties to the table, and helped convince the reluctant Palestinians by getting support for direct talks from Egypt and Jordan.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-ap090110-57)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-nyt-me-test-58) The aim of the talks was to forge the framework of a final agreement within one year, although general expectations of a success were fairly low. The talks aimed to put the Israeli–Palestinian conflict to an official end by forming a two-state solution for the Jewish and Palestinian peoples, promoting the idea of everlasting peace, and putting an official halt to any further land claims, as well as accepting the rejection of any forceful retribution if violence should recur. [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas") and [Hezbollah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hezbollah "Hezbollah"), however, threatened violence, especially if either side seemed likely to compromise in order to reach an agreement. As a result, the Israeli government publicly stated that peace couldn't exist even if both sides signed the agreement, due to the stance taken by Hamas and Hezbollah. The US was therefore compelled to re-focus on eliminating the threat posed by the stance of Hamas and Hezbollah as part of the direct talks process. Israel, for its part, was skeptical that a final agreement would change the situation, as Hamas and Hezbollah would still get support to fuel new violence. In addition, the Israeli government rejected any possible agreement with Palestine as long as it refuses to recognize Israel as a Jewish state.

Since 1982, the mainstream within the PLO had shown interest in mutual recognition and a Palestinian state.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-59) During the 2010 talks, Palestinian Authority President [Mahmoud Abbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Abbas "Mahmoud Abbas") said that the Palestinians and Israel had agreed on the principle of a land swap, but Israel had yet to confirm. The issue of the ratio of land Israel would give to the Palestinians in exchange for keeping settlement blocs was an issue of dispute, with the Palestinians demanding that the ratio be 1:1, and Israel offering less.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-60) In April 2012, Mahmoud Abbas sent a letter to [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") reiterating that for peace talks to resume, Israel must stop settlement building in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and accept the 1967 borders as a basis for a two-state solution.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-61)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-62) In May 2012, Abbas reiterated his readiness to engage with the Israelis if they propose "anything promising or positive".[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-63) Netanyahu replied to Abbas' April letter less than a week later and, for the first time, officially recognised the right for Palestinians to have their own state, though as before[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-64) he declared it would have to be demilitarised,[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-65) and said his new national unity government furnished a new opportunity to renew negotiations and move forward.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-66)

### 2013–14 talks

Main article: [2013–2014 Israeli–Palestinian peace talks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%932014_Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_talks "2013–2014 Israeli–Palestinian peace talks")

Direct negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians began on 29 July 2013 following an attempt by United States Secretary of State [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") to restart the peace process.

[Martin Indyk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Indyk "Martin Indyk") of the Brookings Institution in Washington, D.C., was appointed by the US to oversee the negotiations. Indyk served as U.S. ambassador to Israel and assistant secretary of state for Near East affairs during the Clinton administration.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-67) [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas"), the Palestinian [government in Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governance_of_the_Gaza_Strip "Governance of the Gaza Strip"), rejected Kerry's announcement, stating that Palestinian president [Mahmoud Abbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Abbas "Mahmoud Abbas") has no legitimacy to negotiate in the name of the Palestinian people.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-68)

The negotiations were scheduled to last up to nine months to reach a final status to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict by mid-2014. The Israeli negotiating team was led by veteran negotiator Justice Minister [Tzipi Livni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzipi_Livni "Tzipi Livni"), while the Palestinian delegation was led by [Saeb Erekat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saeb_Erekat "Saeb Erekat"), also a former negotiator. Negotiations started in Washington, DC[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-wapo-69) and were slated to move to the [King David Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_David_Hotel "King David Hotel") in Jerusalem and finally to Hebron.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-70) A deadline was set for establishing a broad outline for an agreement by 29 April 2014. On the expiry of the deadline, negotiations collapsed, with the US Special Envoy Indyk reportedly assigning blame mainly to Israel. The [US State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") insisted no one side was to blame but that "both sides did things that were incredibly unhelpful".[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-71)

Israel reacted angrily to the [Fatah–Hamas Gaza Agreement of 23 April 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Fatah%E2%80%93Hamas_Agreements "2014 Fatah–Hamas Agreements"), whose main purpose was reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas, the formation of a Palestinian unity government, and the holding of new elections.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-bbc20140423-72) Israel halted peace talks with the Palestinians, saying it "will not negotiate with a Palestinian government backed by Hamas, a terrorist organization that calls for Israel's destruction", and threatened sanctions against the Palestinian Authority,[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-ynetnews20140424-73)[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-guardian_halts_peace-74) including a previously announced Israeli plan to unilaterally deduct Palestinian debts to Israeli companies from the tax revenue Israel collects for the PA.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-75) Israeli Prime Minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") accused Abbas of sabotaging peace efforts. He said that Abbas cannot have peace with both Hamas and Israel and has to choose.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-guardian_landmark_pact-76)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-france24_rival_leaderships-77) Abbas said the deal did not contradict their commitment to peace with Israel on the basis of a two-state solution[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-78) and assured reporters that any unity government would recognize Israel, be non-violent, and bound to previous PLO agreements.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-79) Shortly after, Israel began implementing economic sanctions against Palestinians and canceled plans to build housing for Palestinians in Area C of the West Bank.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-80) Abbas also threatened to dissolve the PA, leaving Israel fully responsible for both the West Bank and Gaza,[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-81) a threat that the PA has not put into effect.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-82)

Notwithstanding Israeli objections and actions, the new [Palestinian Unity Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_unity_government_of_2014 "Palestinian unity government of 2014") was formed on 2 June 2014.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-ynetnews20140424-73)

### Abbas' 2014 peace plan

On 3 September 2014, Abbas presented a new proposal for the peace process to John Kerry.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-83)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-reject-84) The plan called for nine months of direct talks followed by a three-year plan for Israel to withdraw to the 1967 lines, leaving East Jerusalem as Palestine's capital.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-85) The resumption of talks was contingent on an Israeli freeze on construction in the West Bank and east Jerusalem,[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Abbasplan-86) as well as the release of the final batch of prisoners from the previous talks.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-87) The first three months of the plan would revolve around the borders and potential land swaps for the 1967 lines. The following six months would focus on issues including refugees, Jerusalem, settlements, security and water.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-88) The US administration rejected the initiative, saying it was opposed to any unilateral move that could negatively impact the Israeli–Palestinian peace process.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-reject-84)

Abbas stated that if Israel rejected the claim he would push for charges against Israel in the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court") over the [2014 Israel–Gaza conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Israel%E2%80%93Gaza_conflict "2014 Israel–Gaza conflict").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Abbasplan-86) Additionally, if rejected, Abbas stated he would turn to the UN Security Council for a unilateral measure for a Palestinian State.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-reject-84) On 1 October 2014, Abbas stated he would be presenting his plan to the UNSC within two to three weeks, with an application to the ICC to follow if it failed to pass the UNSC.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-89) Later that month as previously threatened, Abbas signed the treaty to join the ICC.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-90) Israel responded by freezing NIS 500 million (US$127 million) in Palestinian tax revenues,[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-91) in response to which, the PA banned the sale in the Palestinian territories of products of six major Israeli companies.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-92)

### Trump plan

Further information: [2020 Trump Israel–Palestine plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Trump_Israel%E2%80%93Palestine_plan "2020 Trump Israel–Palestine plan")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Trump_Peace_Plan_Map.jpg/250px-Trump_Peace_Plan_Map.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trump_Peace_Plan_Map.jpg) Trump plan map

Following the inauguration of US President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in January 2017, a period of uncertainty regarding a new peace initiative began. In early 2018, some media sources reported that the new administration was preparing a new peace initiative for an Israeli-Palestinian deal. The White House unveiled the economic part of the Trump initiative, titled _Peace to Prosperity: The Economic Plan_, in June 2019,[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-93) and the political portion of the plan in January 2020. Palestinian leaders boycotted and condemned the [Bahrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain "Bahrain") conference in late June 2019 at which the economic plan was unveiled.

In December 2017, Palestinian president [Mahmoud Abbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Abbas "Mahmoud Abbas") cut ties with the Trump administration after [United States recognition of Jerusalem as capital of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_recognition_of_Jerusalem_as_capital_of_Israel "United States recognition of Jerusalem as capital of Israel"). The Trump administration further raised Palestinians' ire when it moved the US embassy to Jerusalem in May 2018, and cut hundreds of millions of dollars in annual aid to the Palestinians, citing the PA's refusal to take part in the administration's peace initiative.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-94)

### Munich group

In February 2020, on the sidelines of the [Munich Security Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Security_Conference "Munich Security Conference"), the foreign ministers of Egypt, France, Germany, and Jordan, the [Munich Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Group "Munich Group"), together discussed peace efforts.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-95) In July, the same quartet issued a statement declaring that "any annexation of Palestinian territories occupied in 1967 would be a violation of international law" and "would have serious consequences for the security and stability of the region and would constitute a major obstacle to efforts aimed at achieving a comprehensive and just peace". The foreign ministers said they "discussed how to restart a fruitful engagement between the Israeli and the Palestinian side, and offer our support in facilitating a path to negotiations".[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-newQ-96)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-97)

Meeting in Jordan on 24 September, the four again called for a resumption of negotiations between the two sides. There will be "no comprehensive and lasting peace without solving the conflict on the basis of the two-state solution", Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman al-Safadi told reporters following the meeting. The four also praised recent deals establishing ties between [Israel and the United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel%E2%80%93United_Arab_Emirates_normalization_agreement "Israel–United Arab Emirates normalization agreement") and [Bahrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain%E2%80%93Israel_normalization_agreement "Bahrain–Israel normalization agreement"). Egypt's [Sameh Shoukry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sameh_Shoukry "Sameh Shoukry") said the deals are an "important development that would lead to more support and interaction in order to reach a comprehensive peace". However, Palestinians see the two accords as a betrayal.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-98)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-99)

On 11 January 2021, the group met in Cairo to discuss "possible steps to advance the peace process in the Middle East and create an environment conducive to the resumption of dialogue between the Palestinians and the Israelis". A joint statement of the quartet confirmed its intention to work with the incoming administration of President-elect Joe Biden. A further meeting is set to be held in Paris.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-100)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-101)

The four met in Paris on 11 March 2021, with [United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Special_Coordinator_for_the_Middle_East_Peace_Process "United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process") [Tor Wennesland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_Wennesland "Tor Wennesland") and the [European Union Special Representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Special_Representative "European Union Special Representative") for the Middle East Peace Process, Susanna Terstal. Their statement emphasized the importance of confidence-building measures to promote dialogue and support the two-state solution, and stated that settlement activities violate international law.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-102)

On 19 February 2021, at the [Munich Security Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Security_Conference "Munich Security Conference"), as well as reaffirming support for a two state solution, the group condemned the expansion of Israeli settlements and the ongoing [Palestinian displacement in East Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_displacement_in_East_Jerusalem "Palestinian displacement in East Jerusalem"), in particular in [Sheikh Jarrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Jarrah_controversy "Sheikh Jarrah controversy").[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-103)

On 22 September 2022, the group met with Josep Borrell, High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, and the United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Tor Wennesland, and in a statement said "with a view to advancing the Middle East Peace Process towards a just, comprehensive and lasting peace on the basis of the two-state solution".[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Sep22-104)

### Quartet developments

Main article: [Quartet on the Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartet_on_the_Middle_East "Quartet on the Middle East")

In July 2016, the Quartet reported:

> The continuing policy of settlement construction and expansion in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, designation of land for exclusive Israeli use, and denial of Palestinian development, including the recent high rate of demolitions, is steadily eroding the viability of the two-state solution. This raises legitimate questions about Israel's long-term intentions, which are compounded by the statements of some Israeli ministers that there should never be a Palestinian state. In fact, the transfer of greater powers and responsibilities to Palestinian civil authority...has effectively been stopped.

It was within this context that the United Nations passed [Security Council Resolution 2334](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_2334 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 2334") in December 2016 in another bid to address the settlement question.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-BayatHerrera2021-105)[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-106) The report was significantly altered to appease Israel and as well as urging Israel to stop its settlement policy, urged Palestine to end incitement to violence.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-107)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-108)

In a speech to the UN General Assembly in September 2018, Mahmoud Abbas called Donald Trump's policies towards Palestinians an "assault on international law". He said the US is "too biased towards Israel", indicating that others could broker talks and that the US could participate as a member of the Middle East peace Quartet.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-109) Abbas reiterated this position at a UN Security Council meeting on 11 February 2020.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-110)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-newQ-96)

As of 16 September 2020, the UN has not been able to gather the consensus necessary for the Quartet or a group of countries linked to the Quartet to meet.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-111)[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-112) On 25 September 2020, at the UN, Abbas called for an international conference early in 2021 to "launch a genuine peace process".[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-113)

On 15 February 2021, the quartet envoys met virtually and agreed to meet regularly to continue their engagement.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-114) On 23 March 2021, the Quartet discussed the reviving of "meaningful negotiations" between Israel and the Palestinians who both need "to refrain from unilateral actions that make a two-state solution more difficult to achieve".[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-115)[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-116)

### Gaza peace plan

Main article: [Gaza peace plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_peace_plan "Gaza peace plan")

See also: [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war")

This section is an excerpt from [Gaza peace plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_peace_plan "Gaza peace plan").\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gaza_peace_plan&action=edit)\]

The [Gaza peace plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_peace_plan "Gaza peace plan"), officially the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, is a multilateral agreement between [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") and [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas") that aims to address the ongoing [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") and broader [Middle Eastern crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Eastern_crisis_(2023%E2%80%93present) "Middle Eastern crisis (2023–present)"). Led by [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), it was negotiated in consultation with many [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world") and [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world") countries. The plan was announced by Trump on September 29, 2025, during a press conference at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") alongside Israeli prime minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu"). It was signed on October 9, coming into effect the following day, and [was endorsed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_2803 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803") by the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") on November 17.

After the 2005 [Israeli disengagement from the Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_disengagement_from_the_Gaza_Strip "Israeli disengagement from the Gaza Strip"), Hamas [won elections in 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Palestinian_legislative_election "2006 Palestinian legislative election") and formed a government, first alone and then in a [grand coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_coalition "Grand coalition") with [Fatah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatah "Fatah"), but later [seized Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaza_(2007) "Battle of Gaza (2007)") in 2007. Since then, repeated clashes with Israel have escalated into [major conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza%E2%80%93Israel_conflict "Gaza–Israel conflict"), culminating in the [October 7 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_7_attacks "October 7 attacks") by Hamas in 2023, which triggered a large-scale [Israeli military campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_invasion_of_the_Gaza_Strip "Israeli invasion of the Gaza Strip") and [genocide in Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_genocide "Gaza genocide"). Interim ceasefires in [late 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Gaza_war_ceasefire "2023 Gaza war ceasefire") and [early 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_2025_Gaza_war_ceasefire "January 2025 Gaza war ceasefire") collapsed.

The Gaza peace plan calls for an immediate [ceasefire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceasefire "Ceasefire"), the return of [all hostages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war_hostage_crisis "Gaza war hostage crisis"), [prisoner exchanges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_exchanges "Prisoner exchanges"), the [demilitarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demilitarisation "Demilitarisation") of the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip"), the deployment of the [International Stabilization Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Stabilization_Force "International Stabilization Force"), [transitional governance by](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_International_Transitional_Authority "Gaza International Transitional Authority") Palestinian [technocrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technocracy "Technocracy") under international supervision, large-scale reconstruction, and a conditional pathway toward acceptance of Palestinian [self-determination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination#The_UN_Charter_and_resolutions "Self-determination") and recognition of [Palestinian statehood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Palestinian_statehood "History of Palestinian statehood"). The plan was met with support from many countries around the world, including [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan"), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_reuters20250930-117) The [State of Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine "Palestine") was not involved in the negotiations, although the governing [Palestinian Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Authority "Palestinian Authority") expressed support for the deal. Prior to Trump's announcement of the plan, Hamas has maintained that it will not disarm without the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_nytimes20250929-118)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_jpost20250928-119)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-120) Upon revealing the peace proposal, Trump gave Hamas a deadline of October 5, 2025, to accept.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_bbc20251003-121) On October 3, in response to the proposal, Hamas agreed to release any remaining hostages in Gaza and to "hand over the administration of the Gaza Strip to a Palestinian body of independent technocrats", though it did not agree to disarm or to forgo influence in Gaza.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_washingtonpost20251003-122)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_economist20251004-123) Analysts have stated that Hamas is not likely to hand over weapons as long as there is no guarantee of Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-124)

On October 8, Trump announced that Israel and Hamas had reached an agreement to begin the first phase of the deal. Under this phase, all living hostages were to be released in exchange for 2,000 Palestinian prisoners, including 250 serving life sentences, within 72 hours of the withdrawal of Israeli forces to pre-designated [lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Line_(Gaza) "Yellow Line (Gaza)") within the Gaza Strip.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-125) The ceasefire went into effect on October 10,[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-126) though there have been numerous attacks since, including the killing of more than 1,060 Palestinians by Israel.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-127) The commencement of the second phase of the plan was announced by US Special Envoy [Steve Witkoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Witkoff "Steve Witkoff") on 14 January 2026,[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_phasetwoannounced-128) but as of May 2026, negotiations have remained stalled due to repeated Israeli attacks since ‌the October ceasefire and disagreements over the plan of Hamas disarmament. Israel stated they will not move forward if they do not see progress on disarmament. Hamas had stated that it will not discuss the second phase of the agreement, which includes disarmament, until Israel fully implements the first phase.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Gaza_peace_plan_timesofisrael20260505-129)[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-130)[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-131) On 6 July, Hamas announced the resignation of [its civil administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip_under_Hamas "Gaza Strip under Hamas") under the Gaza peace plan, breaking the limbo that had existed since January 2026.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-132)
