### Palestinian views on the peace process

Main article: [Palestinian views on the peace process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_views_on_the_peace_process "Palestinian views on the peace process")

Palestinians trace the conflict's origins and peace efforts to the 1948 Arab–Israeli war and the issue of Palestinian refugees.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Pappe,_I._2004-133) By the late 1970s, most Palestinian leaders and Arab states had come to support a two-state solution alongside Israel.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-mishal_sela-7) The [PLO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_Liberation_Organization "Palestine Liberation Organization") gradually moved from calls for the "destruction" of Israel toward acceptance of coexistence with Israel,[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-134) though the right of return for refugees has remained central to Palestinian positions.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-135) Continuing Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank has been cited by Palestinians and international observers as a major obstacle to realizing a future Palestinian state.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-136)

### Israeli views on the peace process

Main article: [Israeli views on the peace process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_views_on_the_peace_process "Israeli views on the peace process")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Flickr_-_Government_Press_Office_%28GPO%29_-_THE_NOBEL_PEACE_PRIZE_LAUREATES_FOR_1994_IN_OSLO..jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Government_Press_Office_%28GPO%29_-_THE_NOBEL_PEACE_PRIZE_LAUREATES_FOR_1994_IN_OSLO..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Government_Press_Office_(GPO)_-_THE_NOBEL_PEACE_PRIZE_LAUREATES_FOR_1994_IN_OSLO..jpg)(right to left) Yitzhak Rabin, [Shimon Peres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimon_Peres "Shimon Peres") and [Yasser Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat "Yasser Arafat") receiving the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") following the [Oslo Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Accords "Oslo Accords")

There are several [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") views of the peace process. Israel's position is that the president of the [Palestinian Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Authority "Palestinian Authority"), Mahmoud Abbas, ought to be the negotiating partner in the peace talks, and not Hamas, which has at times engaged with Israel in escalations of the conflict and attacks Israel's civilian population.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-137)[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-138)

The violence of the [second intifada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa_Intifada "Al-Aqsa Intifada") and the political success of [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas") had convinced many Israelis that peace and negotiation are not possible and that a two-state system is not the answer.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Slater,_J._2001,_Pages_171-199-139) Since the break down of negotiations, security has played a less important role in Israeli concerns, trailing behind employment, corruption, housing and other pressing issues.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Sara_M._Roy-140) Israeli policy had reoriented to focus on managing the conflict and the associated occupation of Palestinian territory, rather than reaching a negotiated solution.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Sara_M._Roy-140)[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaconi2018-141)[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-William_L._Cleveland_and_Martin_Bunt,_William_L._Cleveland,_Martin_Bunt...-142)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-143)[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-144) Hardliners believe that Israel should annex all Palestinian territory, or at least all minus the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip").[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Slater,_J._2001,_Pages_171-199-139) Israelis view the peace process as hindered and near impossible due to [terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism") on the part of Palestinians and do not trust Palestinian leadership to maintain control.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Slater,_J._2001,_Pages_171-199-139) According to Slater, during the time when [Yitzhak Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Rabin "Yitzhak Rabin") was in office, the Palestinian Authority largely fulfilled its commitment to combat terrorism. Palestinian security forces, led by Yasser Arafat, collaborated closely with Israeli security forces. This cooperation included joint patrols and efforts to identify and detain extremists and suspected terrorists, often based on lists provided by the Israelis.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-145) Pedahzur describes suicide terrorism as influencing the Israeli public's view of the value of maintaining forces on the ground in the occupied Gaza Strip.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-146) A common theme throughout the peace process has been a feeling that the Palestinians give too little in their peace offers.

Some Israelis believe that the Gaza Strip is fully controlled by the Hamas who do not want peace with Israel.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-147) According to the Israeli view, this limits the ability of the Palestinians to make peace with Israel and enforce it over the long term. Furthermore, in the Israeli view, a violent overtake of the West Bank by the Hamas as a result of the creation of an unstable new state is likely.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-148) Lastly, rhetoric from high-ranking Fatah officials promising a full, literal [Palestinian right of return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_right_of_return "Palestinian right of return") into Israel (a position no Israeli government can accept without destroying the Jewish character of Israel) makes peace negotiations more difficult.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-149)\[ _[pageneeded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\]

### US views on the peace process

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country%2C_adjusted_for_inflation%2C_1946-2022.png/330px-Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country%2C_adjusted_for_inflation%2C_1946-2022.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country,_adjusted_for_inflation,_1946-2022.png) Total US foreign aid to Israel compared to other countries. 1946–2022.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-aid-150)

US officials, citizens and lobbying groups hold divergent views on the peace process. All recent US Presidents have maintained a policy that Israel must give up some of the land that it conquered in the [1967 War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War "Six-Day War") in order to achieve peace;[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-151) that the Palestinians must actively prevent terrorism; and that Israel has an unconditional [right to exist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_exist "Right to exist"). Presidents [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") publicly supported the creation of a new [Palestinian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_state "Palestinian state") out of most of the current Palestinian territories, based on the idea of [self-determination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination "Self-determination") for the Palestinian people,[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-152) and [President Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") continued that policy.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-153) [Secretary of State Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_Hillary_Clinton "Secretary of State Hillary Clinton") thought that peace can only be achieved through direct, bilateral negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-154) Obama outlined the pursuit of the [two-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-state_solution "Two-state solution") as American policy for achieving Palestinian aspirations, Israeli security, and a measure of stability in the Middle East.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-155)

According to the sociologist [Mervin Verbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mervin_Verbit "Mervin Verbit"), [American Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jews "American Jews") are "more right than left" on peace process issues. Verbit found that [surveys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_poll "Opinion poll") of American Jews often reflect the view of the poll's sponsors. Often it is the wording of the survey questions that bias the outcome (a headline illustrating this point reads "ADL poll shows higher support for Israel than did survey by dovish J Street"). Using survey data from the [American Jewish Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jewish_Committee "American Jewish Committee") where findings could not be attributed to wording biases, Verbit found American Jews took a rightward shift following the collapse of the Camp David talks in 2000, and the 9/11 attacks in 2001.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-156)

The Jordanian-American journalist [Rami George Khouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rami_George_Khouri "Rami George Khouri") opines that United States is not willing to mediate a just Israeli-Palestinian peace; instead, to protect Israel, it sends military equipment to the country, which prevents any attempt to address the root causes of tension in the region. This has generated popular [resistance groups across the Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_of_Resistance "Axis of Resistance") that routinely attack both US and Israeli targets.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-157)

## Major issues between the two sides: 2000–2019

See also: [Israeli–Palestinian conflict §Issues in dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict#Issues_in_dispute "Israeli–Palestinian conflict"), and [History of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "History of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Cia-is-map2.png/250px-Cia-is-map2.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cia-is-map2.png) The [1949 Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Israel) "Green Line (Israel)") borders

The core issues of the conflict are borders, the status of settlements in the West Bank, the status of east Jerusalem, the Palestinian refugee right of return, and security.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-158)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-quandt_pp-159)[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-Shlomo_Avineri-160) With the PLO's recognition of Israel's right to exist in 1982,[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-161) the international community with the main exception of the United States and Israel[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-162)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-163) has been in consensus on a framework for resolving the conflict on the basis of international law.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-deluge-164) Various UN bodies and the ICJ have supported this position;[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-deluge-164)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-quandt_pp-159) every year, the UN General Assembly votes almost unanimously in favor of a resolution titled "Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine". This resolution consistently affirms the illegality of the Israeli settlements, the annexation of East Jerusalem, and the principle of the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war. It also emphasizes the need for an Israeli withdrawal from the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967 and the need for a just resolution to the refugee question on the basis of UN resolution 194.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-y303-165)

There remain some activists on the Palestinian side who claim that there are still some positive signs on the Palestinian side, and that Israel should use these to cultivate some positive interactions with the Palestinians, even in spite of Hamas's basic opposition to the existence of the Jewish State. Since mid-June 2007, Israel has cooperated with Palestinian security forces in the West Bank at unprecedented levels, thanks in part to United States-sponsored training, equipping, and funding of the Palestinian National Security Forces and Presidential Guard.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-166)

A further concern is whether, as a result of this security argument, Israel will in fact allow the Palestinian community to emerge as a viable and sovereign political unit, a viable and contiguous state. There are also various economic and political restrictions placed on Palestinian people, activities, and institutions which have had a detrimental effect on the Palestinian economy and quality of life.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-167) Israel has said repeatedly that these restrictions are necessary due to security concerns, and in order to counteract ongoing efforts which promote terrorism which incite opposition to Israel's existence and rights as a country. The key obstacle therefore remains the Israeli demand for security versus Palestinian claims for rights and statehood.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-168)

Furthermore, the identification of 'Palestinian' with 'terrorist' can be construed as problematic, and Sayigh argues that this association is used as a rationale for maintaining the status quo, and that only by recognising the status of Jewish immigrants as 'settlers' can we conceptually move forwards.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-169)

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Graffiti_on_the_Bethlehem_wall_05.jpg/250px-Graffiti_on_the_Bethlehem_wall_05.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graffiti_on_the_Bethlehem_wall_05.jpg) [Israeli West Bank barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_West_Bank_barrier "Israeli West Bank barrier") in [Bethlehem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem "Bethlehem")

Nevertheless, there is a range of ulterior motives for Israel's denial of Palestinian statehood. If Palestine were declared a state, then immediately, Israel, by its present occupation of the West Bank, will be in breach of the United Nations Charter. Palestine, as a state, could legitimately call upon the inherent right of individual or collective self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter to remove Israel from the occupied territories. Palestine, as a state, would be able to accede to international conventions and bring legal action against Israel on various matters. Palestine could accede to various international human rights instruments, such as the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. It could even join the International Criminal Court and file cases against Israel for war crimes. It would be a tinderbox of a situation that is highly likely to precipitate conflict in the Middle East.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-170)

There is a lively debate around the shape that a lasting peace settlement would take (see for example the [One-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-state_solution "One-state solution") and [Two-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-state_solution "Two-state solution")). Authors like Cook have argued that the one-state solution is opposed by Israel because the very nature of Zionism and Jewish nationalism calls for a Jewish majority state, whilst the two-state solution would require the difficult relocation of half a million Jewish settlers living in the West Bank and East Jerusalem.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-171) The Palestinian leaders such as [Salam Fayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salam_Fayyad "Salam Fayyad") have rejected calls for a [binational state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binational_state "Binational state") or unilateral declaration of statehood. As of 2010, only a minority of Palestinians and Israelis support the one-state solution.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-172) Interest in a one-state solution is growing as of 2012[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process&action=edit), however, as the two-state approach fails to accomplish a final agreement.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-173)[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-174)

## Alternative peace proposals

Another approach was taken by a team of negotiators led by former [Israeli Justice Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Justice_Minister "Israeli Justice Minister") [Yossi Beilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yossi_Beilin "Yossi Beilin"), and former Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo following two and a half years of secret negotiations. On 1 December 2003, the two parties signed an unofficial suggested plan for peace in Geneva (dubbed the [Geneva Accord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Accord_(2003) "Geneva Accord (2003)")). In sharp contrast to the road map, it is not a plan for a temporary ceasefire but a comprehensive and detailed solution aiming at all the issues at stake, in particular, Jerusalem, the settlements and the refugee problem.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-175) It was met with bitter denunciation by the Israeli government and many Palestinians, with the Palestinian Authority staying non-committal, but it was warmly welcomed by many European governments and some significant elements of the Bush Administration, including Secretary of State [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell").

Yet another approach was proposed by a number of parties inside and outside Israel: a " [binational solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binational_solution "Binational solution")" whereby Israel would formally annex the Palestinian territories but would make the Palestinian Arabs citizens in a unitary secular state. Championed by [Edward Said](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Said "Edward Said") and [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") professor [Tony Judt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Judt "Tony Judt"), the suggestion aroused both interest and condemnation. It was not actually a new idea, dating back as far as the 1920s, but it was given extra prominence by the growing [demographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic "Demographic") issues raised by a rapidly expanding Arab population in Israel and the territories.

The [Elon Peace Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Peace_Plan "Elon Peace Plan") is a solution for the Arab-Israeli conflict proposed in 2002 by former minister [Binyamin Elon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binyamin_Elon "Binyamin Elon"). The plan advocates the formal annexation of West Bank and Gaza by Israel and that Palestinians will become either [Jordanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") citizens or permanent residents in Israel so long as they remained peaceful and law-abiding residents. All these actions should be done in agreement with Jordan and the Palestinian population. This solution is tied to the [demographics of Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Jordan "Demographics of Jordan") where it is claimed that Jordan is essentially already the Palestinian state, as it has so many Palestinian refugees and their descendants.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-176)

An attempt to change the rules was made by [Condoleezza Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condoleezza_Rice "Condoleezza Rice") and Tzipi Livni when they brought forth the concept of a shelf agreement.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-177) The idea was to disengage the linkage between negotiations and actions on the ground. In theory this would allow negotiations until a "shelf agreement" defining peace would be obtained. Such an agreement would not entail implementation. It would just describe what peace is. It would stay on the shelf but eventually will guide the implementation. The difficulty with this notion is that it creates a dis-incentive for Israel to reach such an agreement. The lack of clarity about what happens after agreement is reached will result in insurmountable pressures on Abbas to demand immediate implementation. However, from the Israeli point of view, the Palestinians are not ready to create a stable state, such an implementation process will almost guarantee instability in the Palestinian areas with a possible Hamas takeover as happened in Gaza.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-178)

This situation brings the process to another impasse. To avoid it some definition of what happens after a shelf agreement is needed. One possible idea by this essay is to agree ahead of time that following attainment of a final status agreement there will be a negotiated detailed and staged implementation agreement which would define a process which would allow the creation of a stable functional Palestinian state in stages and over time.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-179) In August 2013, an indication that such an idea can be acceptable to the Palestinians was given by Mahmud Abbas in a meeting with Meretz MK-s.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-180) In the meeting Abbas stated "that there cannot be an interim agreement but only a final status deal that can be implemented in stages".

[A Land for All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Land_for_All_(organization) "A Land for All (organization)") (also known as "Two States, One Homeland"),[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-:0-181) an Israeli-Palestinian political initiative, proposes a [confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederation "Confederation") of two sovereign, democratic states, modeled on the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union").[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-:4-182)[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-183) Borders along the 1967 [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Israel) "Green Line (Israel)") would be open, with some controls, and residency of Palestinians in Israel and Israelis in Palestine would be allowed to gradually increase, by mutual agreement. Their proposal was presented at the 2025 UN High-Level Conference on "The Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution."[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-184) In November, 2025, their proposal was adopted by [Standing Together](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Together_(movement) "Standing Together (movement)"), a social justice movement of Jewish and Palestinian citizens of Israel.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-185)

## Joint economic effort and development

Main article: [Arab–Israeli peace projects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_peace_projects "Arab–Israeli peace projects")

Despite the long history of conflict between Israelis and Palestinians, a number of peace initiatives that respect the rights of both peoples have been undertaken by people on both sides.

In March 2007, [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") proposed a plan for peace based on common economic development and effort, rather than on continuous wrangling over land. Both sides stated their support.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_peace_process#cite_note-186) This became the [Peace Valley plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Valley_plan "Peace Valley plan"), a joint effort of the Israeli, Palestinian and Jordanian governments to promote economic cooperation, and new business initiatives which can help both sides work together, and create a better diplomatic atmosphere and better economic conditions. It is mainly designed to foster efforts in the private sector, once governments provide the initial investment and facilities.
